PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.

Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.

California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.

Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.

I'm also pulling the October PPIC poll numbers for Prop 42, since the September figure of 54% support may have shifted. I also want to check the Berkeley IGS data, which seems to show opposition climbing from 34% to 45%, and see whether the LA Times figure of a 9-point lead refers to an earlier poll.

I'm weighing whether Prop 42 is more likely to pass or fail: the late-October Berkeley poll has it at 43% yes and 45% no, while the October PPIC poll seems to show a narrow yes majority, so the outcome looks uncertain. Ballot measures polling under 50% this late often fail, but the yes side has heavy spending and "protect retirement savings" messaging that polls well. I'm also considering how Prop 42 interacts with Prop 40, since the measure with more votes would override the other.

I'm checking the Secretary of State's contributions page to see how much the "Yes on 42" committee has raised compared to the opposition. Endorsements look split: Newsom and several labor and firefighter groups back Prop 42, while Bernie Sanders, SEIU-UHW, the state Democratic Party, and the teachers' union oppose it. I still need to see where the gubernatorial candidates stand on it.

Ballot measures that poll below 50% this late often fail, and constitutional amendments tend to face a harder road in California. The "protect retirement savings" framing could still hold support, and the No side may also have substantial money behind it.

I'm turning to the latest PPIC October poll on Prop 42 to see whether its numbers held up against the September result.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

Support for a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/23/election-2026-california-billionaires-tax-two-competing-measures/) is waning among California voters, according to a new independent poll released this week.
Proposition 40, a highly contentious November ballot measure, has the support of 46% of likely voters in the latest survey from the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) — down from last month’s poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/15/poll-california-voters-back-billionaire-tax-and-measures-that-could-block-it/), which showed it had majority support with 52% of likely voters in favor.
In the latest poll, which was conducted between Oct. 16 and 22 by the San Francisco-based nonpartisan research group, 52% of likely voters were opposed and 2% were undecided. The initiative also saw a 9-percentage-point decline in support among likely Bay Area voters, from 58% in support last month to 49% in support in the latest survey.
The PPIC surveyed 1,086 likely voters and the poll had a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
Proposed by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, the measure would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. The Legislative Analyst’s Office projects that Proposition 40 will raise “tens of billions” for healthcare and food assistance over the next five years.
RELATED: Inside the billionaires’ war against California’s proposed wealth tax (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/inside-the-billionaires-war-against-californias-proposed-wealth-tax/)
Wealthy opponents of the initiative have launched a massive spending blitz in recent months as they campaign against Prop. 40, while also boosting two countermeasures — Propositions 41 and 42. If Proposition 41 or 42 passes and receives more ‘yes’ votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax could be blocked even if voters approve it. Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures.

Prop. 41, which would require the state auditor to review proposed special taxes before they’re placed on the ballot and void taxes that don’t comply with the state spending limit, fell below the majority line in the latest PPIC poll, with 48% of voters in support and 49% opposed. Last month’s poll found that 51% of voters supported the initiative, while 44% were opposed.
Prop. 42, which would prohibit new state personal property taxes, still had a majority support, 51%, in the latest survey, but was down from 54% support last month.
Mark Baldassare, PPIC’s statewide survey director, said in an interview that voters have more information about the three measures, including the supporters and the opponents. For Prop. 40, Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, the California Nurses Association, and Rep. Ro Khanna are listed as some of the supporters in the state voter guide, while Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor — former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and former Fox News host Steve Hilton — are listed as opponents.
Baldassare said that voters are “not convinced that this is the right way to tax the wealth now.”
“Most Californians still say they want to tax the wealthy, but the energy around taxing the wealthy has now kind of moved over to Prop. 3, which is the extension of the tax on high incomes in California,” he added, noting that the initiative, which would extend a tax that funds education, had the support of 58% of likely voters.
Will voters pass CEQA reform?
More voters now are opposed than support a measure that would overhaul the state’s landmark environmental review law (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/04/proposition-45-a-solution-to-build-more-housing-or-a-loophole-for-developers/) — the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA. In the latest poll, 50% of voters oppose the initiative, while 46% of likely voters are in support, compared to the September survey where 46% of voters opposed the measure and 49% were in favor.
The initiative, which was placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce would slim down environmental review and set a 365-day limit on “essential projects,” which includes reservoirs, desalination plants, housing subdivisions, roads, solar farms, battery storage facilities and broadband infrastructure. It would also require courts to make a decision within 270 days on any lawsuits filed under CEQA, which has often been used to block the construction of new housing and other developments.
“Californians are really divided about giving up environmental protections through Prop. 45,” Baldassare said. “I think the outcome on that continues to be very much in doubt for which way it will go.”
Supporters of the measure, which include the Bay Area Council, the California Business Roundtable and the California Wind Energy Association, argue that the initiative would help speed up development and cut red tape. But opponents, which includes the Sierra Club, the California Democratic Party and the California Nurses Association, argue that it would fast track projects that are heavy polluters.
Voter ID, higher tax threshold trail in poll
Out of the 14 statewide measures on the November ballot, the largest segment of likely voters polled, 23%, said that Proposition 39, which would institute voter ID in California (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/), was the ballot measure they were most interested in.
Opposition to Prop. 39 stood at 58% of likely voters, compared with 55% in last month’s survey. 41% of likely voters said they would support the initiative and 1% were undecided.
Voters were heavily divided along partisan lines, with 84% of Democrats opposing the measure and 82% of Republicans in support as the GOP has made voter ID one of its key issues nationwide.
“The overall numbers and the fact that a majority say ‘no’ really reflects the hyper-partisanship that we see in the electorate today because Republicans have very different feelings than Democrats do about Prop. 39,” Baldassare said.
The initiative is backed by Reform California, a statewide organization led by state Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican, and is opposed by the California Democratic Party and Democratic Party officials including U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla and former Health Secretary and gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra.

Support for a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/23/election-2026-california-billionaires-tax-two-competing-measures/) is waning among California voters, according to a new independent poll released this week.
Proposition 40, a highly contentious November ballot measure, has the support of 46% of likely voters in the latest survey from the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) — down from last month’s poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/15/poll-california-voters-back-billionaire-tax-and-measures-that-could-block-it/), which showed it had majority support with 52% of likely voters in favor.
In the latest poll, which was conducted between Oct. 16 and 22 by the San Francisco-based nonpartisan research group, 52% of likely voters were opposed and 2% were undecided. The initiative also saw a 9-percentage-point decline in support among likely Bay Area voters, from 58% in support last month to 49% in support in the latest survey.
The PPIC surveyed 1,086 likely voters and the poll had a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
Proposed by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, the measure would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. The Legislative Analyst’s Office projects that Proposition 40 will raise “tens of billions” for healthcare and food assistance over the next five years.
RELATED: Inside the billionaires’ war against California’s proposed wealth tax (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/inside-the-billionaires-war-against-californias-proposed-wealth-tax/)
Wealthy opponents of the initiative have launched a massive spending blitz in recent months as they campaign against Prop. 40, while also boosting two countermeasures — Propositions 41 and 42. If Proposition 41 or 42 passes and receives more ‘yes’ votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax could be blocked even if voters approve it. Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures.

Prop. 41, which would require the state auditor to review proposed special taxes before they’re placed on the ballot and void taxes that don’t comply with the state spending limit, fell below the majority line in the latest PPIC poll, with 48% of voters in support and 49% opposed. Last month’s poll found that 51% of voters supported the initiative, while 44% were opposed.
Prop. 42, which would prohibit new state personal property taxes, still had a majority support, 51%, in the latest survey, but was down from 54% support last month.
Mark Baldassare, PPIC’s statewide survey director, said in an interview that voters have more information about the three measures, including the supporters and the opponents. For Prop. 40, Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, the California Nurses Association, and Rep. Ro Khanna are listed as some of the supporters in the state voter guide, while Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor — former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and former Fox News host Steve Hilton — are listed as opponents.
Baldassare said that voters are “not convinced that this is the right way to tax the wealth now.”
“Most Californians still say they want to tax the wealthy, but the energy around taxing the wealthy has now kind of moved over to Prop. 3, which is the extension of the tax on high incomes in California,” he added, noting that the initiative, which would extend a tax that funds education, had the support of 58% of likely voters.
Will voters pass CEQA reform?
More voters now are opposed than support a measure that would overhaul the state’s landmark environmental review law (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/04/proposition-45-a-solution-to-build-more-housing-or-a-loophole-for-developers/) — the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA. In the latest poll, 50% of voters oppose the initiative, while 46% of likely voters are in support, compared to the September survey where 46% of voters opposed the measure and 49% were in favor.
The initiative, which was placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce would slim down environmental review and set a 365-day limit on “essential projects,” which includes reservoirs, desalination plants, housing subdivisions, roads, solar farms, battery storage facilities and broadband infrastructure. It would also require courts to make a decision within 270 days on any lawsuits filed under CEQA, which has often been used to block the construction of new housing and other developments.
“Californians are really divided about giving up environmental protections through Prop. 45,” Baldassare said. “I think the outcome on that continues to be very much in doubt for which way it will go.”
Supporters of the measure, which include the Bay Area Council, the California Business Roundtable and the California Wind Energy Association, argue that the initiative would help speed up development and cut red tape. But opponents, which includes the Sierra Club, the California Democratic Party and the California Nurses Association, argue that it would fast track projects that are heavy polluters.
Voter ID, higher tax threshold trail in poll
Out of the 14 statewide measures on the November ballot, the largest segment of likely voters polled, 23%, said that Proposition 39, which would institute voter ID in California (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/08/03/california-voter-id-prop-39-both-sides-sue/), was the ballot measure they were most interested in.
Opposition to Prop. 39 stood at 58% of likely voters, compared with 55% in last month’s survey. 41% of likely voters said they would support the initiative and 1% were undecided.
Voters were heavily divided along partisan lines, with 84% of Democrats opposing the measure and 82% of Republicans in support as the GOP has made voter ID one of its key issues nationwide.
“The overall numbers and the fact that a majority say ‘no’ really reflects the hyper-partisanship that we see in the electorate today because Republicans have very different feelings than Democrats do about Prop. 39,” Baldassare said.
The initiative is backed by Reform California, a statewide organization led by state Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican, and is opposed by the California Democratic Party and Democratic Party officials including U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla and former Health Secretary and gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra.

Support for a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/23/election-2026-california-billionaires-tax-two-competing-measures/) is waning among California voters, according to a new independent poll released this week.
Proposition 40, a highly contentious November ballot measure, has the support of 46% of likely voters in the latest survey from the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) — down from last month’s poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/15/poll-california-voters-back-billionaire-tax-and-measures-that-could-block-it/), which showed it had majority support with 52% of likely voters in favor.
In the latest poll, which was conducted between Oct. 16 and 22 by the San Francisco-based nonpartisan research group, 52% of likely voters were opposed and 2% were undecided. The initiative also saw a 9-percentage-point decline in support among likely Bay Area voters, from 58% in support last month to 49% in support in the latest survey.
The PPIC surveyed 1,086 likely voters and the poll had a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
Proposed by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, the measure would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. The Legislative Analyst’s Office projects that Proposition 40 will raise “tens of billions” for healthcare and food assistance over the next five years.
RELATED: Inside the billionaires’ war against California’s proposed wealth tax (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/inside-the-billionaires-war-against-californias-proposed-wealth-tax/)
Wealthy opponents of the initiative have launched a massive spending blitz in recent months as they campaign against Prop. 40, while also boosting two countermeasures — Propositions 41 and 42. If Proposition 41 or 42 passes and receives more ‘yes’ votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax could be blocked even if voters approve it. Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures.
