Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . es across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50 percent across regions.
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.

KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. Next I'm checking the Berkeley IGS October poll, which shows 43% yes, 45% no, and 12% undecided, and I want its partisan breakdown from the report itself.

Next I'm pulling up the Berkeley IGS report to get its partisan breakdown, and I'll also look for any newer Prop 42 polling. Given the Democratic-leaning midterm environment, I'm weighing how the partisan makeup of the likely electorate could shift the No side's standing.

Weighting the Berkeley and PPIC samples by size puts the Yes side at about 46.4% and No at about 45.8%, which is essentially a tie. Berkeley has around 8% undecided and PPIC about 2%, and undecided voters in California ballot measures have tended to break No, so there's a slight lean toward No. Yes also holds a large spending edge, roughly 5.6 to 1 as of October 22, and I'm considering how much that could matter.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side's roughly 5.6-to-1 spending edge will translate into votes, since the research on ballot measures suggests spending has less effect when the opposition is generic. I also want to check whether Becerra and Hilton have taken positions on Prop 42, because the No coalition's make-up matters here.

I'm weighing whether the "prohibits new taxes" framing will carry voters, since such measures usually poll well in California. But the opposition is hammering it as a billionaire-funded trick meant to undo the billionaire tax, and once voters learn that purpose, support seems to erode, with Berkeley's DiCamillo finding opposition grows among those who know the intent. I'm also trying to recall how past California measures placed as poison pills against other measures have fared.

I'm checking the past Prop 33, 36 and 32 polls against their results, which suggests undecided voters tend to break No in the final weeks. Prop 42's PPIC support dropped from 54% to 51% and its Berkeley numbers from 43/34 to 43/45, which looks bad for the Yes side.

I'm looking at how the Yes side's spending could keep pushing voters toward a yes in the final weeks, and whether the No side will answer with its own money. On the No side, the labor and SEIU contributions are tallied as opposition to Prop 42, and the SEIU committee's $21.2 million is what makes up most of the $22.7 million total.

The $22.7M opposition total is mostly one committee, the SEIU's $21.2M, while the Yes side has about $128M behind it. I want the Berkeley partisan breakdown next, so I'll pull the IGS report and check the LA Times voter guide for more on Prop 42's arguments and any newer polling.

I'm looking for any post-election results on Prop 42, checking whether early returns are out, and searching for coverage of Prop 40 and the billionaire tax outcome as well.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

Meet the Berkeley IGS Poll Director
Read Mark DiCamillo's bio here. (https://igs.berkeley.edu/people/mark-dicamillo)
The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).
IGS Poll (2016 - current) and California Field Poll data (1950's to 2015) can be downloaded from UC Berkeley Dataverse (https://datasets.lib.berkeley.edu/dataverse/igs).

Meet the Berkeley IGS Poll Director
Read Mark DiCamillo's bio here. (https://igs.berkeley.edu/people/mark-dicamillo)
The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).
IGS Poll (2016 - current) and California Field Poll data (1950's to 2015) can be downloaded from UC Berkeley Dataverse (https://datasets.lib.berkeley.edu/dataverse/igs).

The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).
IGS Poll (2016 - current) and California Field Poll data (1950's to 2015) can be downloaded from UC Berkeley Dataverse (https://datasets.lib.berkeley.edu/dataverse/igs).

California's Prop 40 billionaire tax could pass and still be blocked if Prop 41 or 42 gets more yes votes
Prop 40 needs a majority to pass, but if Prop 41 or Prop 42 gets more yes votes, the billionaire tax could be stopped in court. The constitutional rule, each measure's conflict clause, the three possible outcomes, the October polls and the dates in the count.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
November 03, 2026

The California billionaire tax, Proposition 40, is being decided on November 3, 2026 against two rival measures, Props 41 and 42, with the most yes votes deciding which prevails.
California's billionaire tax has to clear two bars today, not one. Proposition 40 (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/), the one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state's billionaires, passes if it gets more yes votes than no votes. It survives only if it also collects more yes votes than Proposition 41 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-41-guide/) and Proposition 42 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-42-guide/), two measures on the same ballot that each declare a tax of Prop 40's kind "in conflict" with them and "null and void" if they win more yes votes.
The rule behind that is Article II, Section 10(b) of the California Constitution, and the state's Voter Information Guide warns (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40.pdf) on Prop 40's page that the measure "could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters." The two most recent polls both put Prop 42 ahead of Prop 40 in yes support: PPIC's October survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf) has Prop 42 at 51% yes and Prop 40 at 46%, and the Berkeley IGS Poll released (https://escholarship.org/content/qt72722408/qt72722408.pdf) on October 29 has them at 43% and 42%, with none of the three measures above 50% in that survey.
This page explains the rule, each measure's conflict clause, the three ways the count can end, the polls and the money, the 60-day lawsuit clock written into Prop 40's own text, and the dates to watch between tonight's first report and certification on December 11. Our 2026 California ballot cheat sheet (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-ballot-cheat-sheet/) puts all 14 measures on one page with a printable PDF, our 2026 California propositions master guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) covers each one in depth, and the voting master guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-voting-master-guide/) covers where and how to vote until 8 p.m.
Article II, Section 10(b) scores conflicting measures by yes votes, not percentages:
The California Constitution provides (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II), in Article II, Section 10(b): "If provisions of two or more measures approved at the same election conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the highest number of affirmative votes shall prevail." Article XVIII, Section 4 applies the same rule to constitutional amendments, and all three of these measures amend the Constitution.
Three features of the rule matter today. It applies only to measures that are "approved," so a measure that fails is out of the comparison. It counts "affirmative votes," meaning raw yes votes, not the yes percentage; a measure that more voters skip can post a higher percentage on fewer votes. And it applies only to provisions that "conflict," a question the Constitution leaves to the courts when the measures' own texts do not settle it.
Props 41 and 42 each declare a tax like Prop 40's "in conflict" with them:
Proposition 41 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-41-guide/) and Proposition 42 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-42-guide/) were filed with the Attorney General on January 12, 2026 by the same proponent, attorney Kurt R. Oneto, two months after SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West filed the billionaire tax. Neither text names Prop 40, billionaires or a wealth tax. Each instead describes a category of tax, states that it applies to measures "on the ballot at the same election," and attaches a conflict clause.
Prop 41's text says (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) that any same-ballot initiative that "contains a state tax that is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation," meaning the Article XIII B appropriations limit, "shall be deemed to be in conflict with this measure," and that if Prop 41 "receives a greater number of affirmative votes, the provisions of this measure shall prevail in their entirety, and all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void." Prop 40's text places (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) its revenue outside that limit.
Prop 42's text uses (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) the same most-votes and null-and-void wording against any same-ballot initiative that would impose "a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings," a phrase it defines to include "financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property," or a tax based on "a status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date." Prop 40 taxes securities, business interests and intellectual property, and it fixes liability on residency as of January 1, 2026 and net worth as of December 31, 2026.

California's billionaire tax has to clear two bars today, not one. It survives only if it also collects more yes votes than Proposition 41 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-41-guide/) and Proposition 42 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-42-guide/), two measures on the same ballot that each declare a tax of Prop 40's kind "in conflict" with them and "null and void" if they win more yes votes.
The rule behind that is Article II, Section 10(b) of the California Constitution, and the state's Voter Information Guide warns (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40.pdf) on Prop 40's page that the measure "could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters." The two most recent polls both put Prop 42 ahead of Prop 40 in yes support: PPIC's October survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf) has Prop 42 at 51% yes and Prop 40 at 46%, and the Berkeley IGS Poll released (https://escholarship.org/content/qt72722408/qt72722408.pdf) on October 29 has them at 43% and 42%, with none of the three measures above 50% in that survey.

The California Constitution provides (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II), in Article II, Section 10(b): "If provisions of two or more measures approved at the same election conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the highest number of affirmative votes shall prevail." Article XVIII, Section 4 applies the same rule to constitutional amendments, and all three of these measures amend the Constitution.
Three features of the rule matter today. It applies only to measures that are "approved," so a measure that fails is out of the comparison. It counts "affirmative votes," meaning raw yes votes, not the yes percentage; a measure that more voters skip can post a higher percentage on fewer votes. And it applies only to provisions that "conflict," a question the Constitution leaves to the courts when the measures' own texts do not settle it.

Oneto, two months after SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West filed the billionaire tax. Neither text names Prop 40, billionaires or a wealth tax. Prop 40's text places (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) its revenue outside that limit.

Prop 40 taxes securities, business interests and intellectual property, and it fixes liability on residency as of January 1, 2026 and net worth as of December 31, 2026.

*The California billionaire tax, Proposition 40, is being decided on November 3, 2026 against two rival measures, Props 41 and 42, with the most yes votes deciding which prevails.*

Democrats make up most of the electorate and largely oppose the measure, along with the state and San Francisco Democratic parties and the labor federation, and I still need to check how the teachers' union stands on 42.

I'm weighing the No side's messaging, the idea that Prop 42 is a billionaire-funded trick, and whether the poison-pill framing tends to lower support once voters learn about it. I also expect undecided voters to lean No, and that a Democratic-leaning electorate with high enthusiasm could make the billionaire-funded argument land.

I'm weighing how the spending gap plays into this: the more the Yes side outspends, the easier it becomes for the No side to frame the measure as billionaire-funded. Yes is still above 50 in PPIC's October poll, though it has slipped from September, while Berkeley's 43 to 45 reads weaker for Yes.

I'm weighing the poll averages now: PPIC has Yes at 51 and Berkeley has No ahead 45 to 43, so the two sit close to even. Undecideds could tilt toward No, but Yes's spending edge and PPIC's lead keep it from being clear-cut.

I'm now recalling how a few recent California measures fared against their late polls: Prop 33 on rent control was polled in the 40s and lost badly, and Prop 32 on the minimum wage was close to even in polling and also failed.

Now I'm going back over how past California measures fared against their final polls, checking whether the ones polling near 50 tended to lose.

I'm recalling how past California measures that polled near 50 percent tended to end up, and the pattern suggests they often lost once support slipped in late polls. That puts Prop 42's roughly 46 to 47 percent average and its downward trend at something like a 35 to 45 percent chance of passing.

I'm weighing the spending gap, where Yes has roughly $128M against $23M for No, since in California the heavier spender usually wins, though the opponents, including labor, may still ramp up in the final weeks. The PPIC poll's 51 percent for Yes keeps the measure in contention despite the late slide.

I'm still weighing whether Prop 42 comes out on top, and the polls point to something close to a coin flip, maybe a 40 to 50 percent chance of passing. The question is which side is more likely to win, and given the close polls and the downward trend, I lean toward No.

How this is built
Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). Is Prop 39 (voter ID) passing?

Is Prop 40 (billionaire tax) passing?

Frequently asked questions
Is Prop 39 (voter ID) passing?
It trails in PPIC (Oct. 16–22: 41% yes, 58% no) and IGS (Oct. 19–25: 37% yes, 57% no, 5% undecided, explicitly printed in Table 2). It led in SurveyUSA (49% yes, 42% no, 10% undecided) and IVP (43% yes, 40% no, 17% undecided). These are polls, not election results.
Is Prop 40 (billionaire tax) passing?
It trails in PPIC (Oct. 16–22: 46% yes, 52% no, 2% don’t know) and IGS (Oct. 19–25: 42% yes, 50% no, 8% undecided). SurveyUSA (Oct. 19–24) had it at 44% yes, 43% no, 13% undecided, a one-point lead within its interval. These are polls, not election results.
Are Props 41 and 42 leading?
Both trail in IGS: Prop 41 is 38% yes and 47% no; Prop 42 is 43% yes and 45% no. PPIC had Prop 42 at 51% yes, 47% no and 2% don’t know. These are polls, not election results.

I'm laying out the Prop 42 polls side by side, with the PPIC and Berkeley IGS results from October and September, and I'm looking at how the yes and no numbers compare across them.

I'm checking whether any other pollster, like IVP/IVC or Emerson, also measured Prop 42, since the ones I've found so far don't show it. The IVP poll I'd noted was about Prop 39 instead, and SurveyUSA doesn't seem to have covered it at all. I'm also weighing how the partisan makeup of the electorate might shape the yes and no split.

I'm comparing the Sept and Oct Berkeley numbers, where the "No" share jumped from 34 to 45 while undecideds fell from 23 to 12. PPIC shows a similar drift toward "No" over the same stretch, and both polls were fielded after Newsom's endorsement.

I'm averaging the two polls to see where things land: Yes comes out around 47 and No around 46, with about 7% undecided. Splitting those undecideds two to one toward No would push the margin slightly further toward No, though the sums don't cleanly add to 100.

I'm working through the averaged numbers: with undecideds split two to one toward No, Yes lands near 49 and No near 51, so the naive average has Yes slightly behind. The On Point model's 50% polling average seems to lean on the September polls, which look less relevant now that the October trend is pointing down, and using only the October polls gives roughly 49.4% for Yes.

I'm weighing the money gap too, with the Yes side spending around $128 million against roughly $23 million for No. In California ballot fights that kind of spending usually matters most on lower-salience measures, though for a high-profile race with heavy advertising it may move opinion as well.

I'm checking the spending side now: the Yes campaign has poured in well over $100 million against roughly $23 million for No, a gap of about five to one. In past California ballot fights, the side with that kind of money has usually won, especially on high-profile measures heavy with advertising.

I'm bringing up recent California ballot fights where the side with a big spending edge on a close measure ended up winning or losing, to see how much the money gap usually matters.

I'm weighing whether big spending wins here, since past California fights like Prop 26 lost despite heavy outside money for the Yes side. The No messaging about a billionaire-funded trick may not reach many voters, while the retirement-savings framing for Yes could land with older, high-turnout voters, and I'm wondering how that plays out among those 55 and older.

I'm weighing how older voters, who make up most of a midterm electorate and back Prop 42 by a wide margin, could tilt the result toward Yes. The PPIC October likely-voter number of 51% also fits that picture, though Berkeley's sample reads differently. Putting it together, I'd put the chance of passage somewhere around 45 to 55 percent, leaning slightly toward caution given the late shift toward No and the money gap.

I'm looking at whether a prediction market like Kalshi or Polymarket has priced Prop 42, since that could show where the odds sit compared with the polls. I'm also checking news analysis from Politico and CalMatters for a read on its chances.

I'm checking whether a prediction market like Kalshi or Polymarket has its own odds on Prop 40, since that could be a useful check on the polls.

By
Daniel Farr (https://nypost.com/author/daniel-farr/)
Published
Oct. 29, 2026, 5:00 a.m. PT

California’s billionaire tax is looking like a long shot, with prediction-market traders betting the controversial measure will go down in flames as voters prepare to decide 14 statewide propositions (https://nypost.com/2026/06/30/us-news/see-the-14-measures-on-californias-november-2026-ballot/) next week.
Kalshi and Polymarket International’s displayed markets put several proposals in strong positions, while others, including a voter ID requirement and a mandate for community health clinics, are drawing much lower passage estimates.
Here’s how the numbers stack up, according to the displayed market odds (https://defirate.com/odds/california-props/):

Housing and infrastructure
Proposition 1 — Housing bonds: Authorizes $11.25 billion for veteran and affordable housing programs. Kalshi: 75% | Polymarket: 89%
Proposition 37 — Homebuyer loans: Creates a state-backed low-cost loan and mortgage program for middle-income buyers of qualified new homes. Kalshi: 91% | Polymarket: 82%

The Kalshi app is displayed on a smartphone. Bloomberg via Getty Images
State finances and elections
Proposition 2 — Rainy Day Fund: Raises deposit limits and the maximum cap for the state’s reserve fund. Kalshi: 92% | Polymarket: 72%
Proposition 4 — Public campaign financing: Repeals the prohibition on public funding for election campaigns. Kalshi: 9% | Polymarket: 22%
Proposition 5 — Recall elections: Changes the recall process for statewide officers by removing the simultaneous successor election. Kalshi: 9% | Polymarket: 26%
Taxes and spending rules
Proposition 3 — High-earner tax: Makes a temporary income tax increase permanent to fund public schools and health care. Kalshi: 95% | Polymarket: 94%
Proposition 40 — Billionaire tax: Imposes a one-time wealth tax on billionaires to fund health care and educational facilities. Kalshi: 25% | Polymarket: 23%
Proposition 41 — Tax spending limits and audits: Restricts new state taxes that fall outside specified spending-limit rules and requires independent audits of special tax revenue. Kalshi: 54% | Polymarket: 59%
Proposition 42 — Property and retroactive taxes: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and retroactive tax legislation. Kalshi: 79% | Polymarket: 80%
Proposition 43 — Local tax votes: Raises the voting threshold for certain local tax increases. Kalshi: 19% | Polymarket: 25%

The Polymarket website. Bloomberg via Getty Images
Voting, health care and the environment
Proposition 39 — Voter ID: Requires government-issued photo identification to vote. Kalshi: 14% | Polymarket: 21%
Proposition 38 — Immunology research bonds: Authorizes $8.4 billion in state bonds for medical research facilities. Kalshi: 82% | Polymarket: 72%
Proposition 44 — Clinic spending: Requires community health clinics to direct at least 90% of revenue toward patient programs and services. Kalshi: 8% | Polymarket: 11%
Proposition 45 — Environmental review: Changes the CEQA review process for designated housing, transit and infrastructure projects. Kalshi: 32% | Polymarket: 37%

Californians can trade on these political outcomes because prediction-market contracts are treated under a different legal and regulatory framework from sports betting.
Federal law classifies prediction markets as financial derivatives rather than sports gambling, allowing platforms such as Kalshi and the US-regulated version of Polymarket to operate under that framework.
The percentages represent market-implied chances of passage, not official forecasts or election results.
They can shift as traders buy and sell contracts, and they do not guarantee how voters will ultimately decide.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

Californians can trade on these political outcomes because prediction-market contracts are treated under a different legal and regulatory framework from sports betting.
Federal law classifies prediction markets as financial derivatives rather than sports gambling, allowing platforms such as Kalshi and the US-regulated version of Polymarket to operate under that framework.

By
Daniel Farr (https://nypost.com/author/daniel-farr/)
Published

California’s billionaire tax is looking like a long shot, with prediction-market traders betting the controversial measure will go down in flames as voters prepare to decide 14 statewide propositions (https://nypost.com/2026/06/30/us-news/see-the-14-measures-on-californias-november-2026-ballot/) next week.
Kalshi and Polymarket International’s displayed markets put several proposals in strong positions, while others, including a voter ID requirement and a mandate for community health clinics, are drawing much lower passage estimates.

Housing and infrastructure
Proposition 1 — Housing bonds: Authorizes $11.25 billion for veteran and affordable housing programs. Kalshi: 75% | Polymarket: 89%
Proposition 37 — Homebuyer loans: Creates a state-backed low-cost loan and mortgage program for middle-income buyers of qualified new homes. Kalshi: 91% | Polymarket: 82%
5
The Kalshi app is displayed on a smartphone. Bloomberg via Getty Images
State finances and elections
Proposition 2 — Rainy Day Fund: Raises deposit limits and the maximum cap for the state’s reserve fund. Kalshi: 92% | Polymarket: 72%
Proposition 4 — Public campaign financing: Repeals the prohibition on public funding for election campaigns. Kalshi: 9% | Polymarket: 22%
Proposition 5 — Recall elections: Changes the recall process for statewide officers by removing the simultaneous successor election. Kalshi: 9% | Polymarket: 26%
Taxes and spending rules
Proposition 3 — High-earner tax: Makes a temporary income tax increase permanent to fund public schools and health care. Kalshi: 95% | Polymarket: 94%
Proposition 40 — Billionaire tax: Imposes a one-time wealth tax on billionaires to fund health care and educational facilities. Kalshi: 25% | Polymarket: 23%
Proposition 41 — Tax spending limits and audits: Restricts new state taxes that fall outside specified spending-limit rules and requires independent audits of special tax revenue. Kalshi: 54% | Polymarket: 59%
Proposition 42 — Property and retroactive taxes: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and retroactive tax legislation. Kalshi: 79% | Polymarket: 80%
Proposition 43 — Local tax votes: Raises the voting threshold for certain local tax increases. Kalshi: 19% | Polymarket: 25%
5
The Polymarket website. Bloomberg via Getty Images
Voting, health care and the environment
Proposition 39 — Voter ID: Requires government-issued photo identification to vote. Kalshi: 14% | Polymarket: 21%
Proposition 38 — Immunology research bonds: Authorizes $8.4 billion in state bonds for medical research facilities. Kalshi: 82% | Polymarket: 72%
Proposition 44 — Clinic spending: Requires community health clinics to direct at least 90% of revenue toward patient programs and services. Kalshi: 8% | Polymarket: 11%
Proposition 45 — Environmental review: Changes the CEQA review process for designated housing, transit and infrastructure projects. Kalshi: 32% | Polymarket: 37%

Californians can trade on these political outcomes because prediction-market contracts are treated under a different legal and regulatory framework from sports betting.
Federal law classifies prediction markets as financial derivatives rather than sports gambling, allowing platforms such as Kalshi and the US-regulated version of Polymarket to operate under that framework.
The percentages represent market-implied chances of passage, not official forecasts or election results.
They can shift as traders buy and sell contracts, and they do not guarantee how voters will ultimately decide.

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

California’s billionaire tax is looking like a long shot, with prediction-market traders betting the controversial measure will go down in flames as voters prepare to decide 14 statewide propositions (https://nypost.com/2026/06/30/us-news/see-the-14-measures-on-californias-november-2026-ballot/) next week.

Californians can trade on these political outcomes because prediction-market contracts are treated under a different legal and regulatory framework from sports betting.
Federal law classifies prediction markets as financial derivatives rather than sports gambling, allowing platforms such as Kalshi and the US-regulated version of Polymarket to operate under that framework.
The percentages represent market-implied chances of passage, not official forecasts or election results.
They can shift as traders buy and sell contracts, and they do not guarantee how voters will ultimately decide.

I'm looking at the prediction-market prices as of the evening of Nov 2: Kalshi has Prop 42 near 56%, Polymarket at 54%, so it reads as a toss-up. The earlier Oct 29 figures, around 79–80%, don't line up with that, which makes me suspect different dates or a big market swing.

The Nov 2 toss-up price looks like a sharp move from the roughly 80% readings on Oct 29, which I'd guess came from the Berkeley poll released that day. Both markets now lean slightly toward Yes, around 55–57%, while the recent polls suggest a tie or a slight No, so I'm weighing which signal to trust.

I'm weighing whether the markets or the polls are the better guide here. Markets on ballot measures are thin and can lean toward the "no new taxes" framing that appeals to their trader base, so I'm doubting that the roughly 55% Yes reading tells the whole story.

I'm weighing the polls against the market prices: the PPIC poll has Yes ahead 51–47, while Berkeley has No ahead 43–45, which averages to roughly a tie among decided voters. I'm also considering whether undecided voters on ballot measures usually break toward No, since that status-quo pattern could move the result away from the market's 55% Yes reading.

I'm weighing whether the Democratic share of the electorate and the early-vote share change how the PPIC and Berkeley numbers should be read, since a turnout model could tilt the Yes lead one way or the other.

I'm weighing the Yes side's pitch about protecting retirement savings and avoiding new taxes against the "poison pill" framing that could make voters balk. Democrats may be getting party cues to vote No, and Republicans and independents leaned Yes in September, so the partisan split matters a lot here.

I'm weighing the cost of the No campaign's late spending against the Yes side's fundraising edge, and checking how Prop 41 has been polling as a comparable measure.

I'm weighing the On Point model's 50.7% Yes estimate against the polls, which suggests Prop 42 is closer to a coin flip than the 56.9% chance the model gives it. Undecided voters on measures like this often break toward No, so the adjusted Yes share could land near 49–50%, and the gap comes down to how On Point averages the September polling.

I'm checking whether the On Point model's Yes lean holds up, since the fundamentals might favor No in a Democratic-leaning midterm, and I'm weighing how the county-level projections fit that picture. I'm also starting to compare how prediction markets and polls diverge on measures like this.

I'm comparing the Oct 29 prices of roughly 79–80% with the Nov 2 figures near 55%, and wondering whether the NY Post numbers were stale or accurate. A drop of about 25 points in four days would fit the Berkeley poll landing on Oct 29 and pulling the market toward No.

I'm checking the defirate snapshots next, since they list Prop 42 at different prices (57% on Kalshi against 92¢ on Polymarket in one listing) and that inconsistency makes me trust the Nov 2 reading of about 55% more than the rest.

The market and the model both put Prop 42's Yes side slightly ahead, around 55–57%, but the polls lean closer to a tie, so I want to check whether anyone has analyzed the outcome directly before deciding which signal to trust. I'm going to look for expert commentary on whether Prop 42 is likely to pass.

I'm going to look for analysis of whether Prop 42 is expected to pass, and I'll check the Politico piece on Newsom's poison-pill problem, since it may cite private polling on the measure.

Newsom’s poison-pill problem
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones)
10/26/2026 09:00 AM EDT
California Gov. Gavin Newsom attends a rally with members of the state's Democratic Party, organized labor, and other advocates in San Francisco, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. | Heather Diehl/AP
DOUBLE TROUBLE — If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to Gavin Newsom . But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible. One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%. And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
Newsom, a likely presidential contender, already has taken considerable political heat (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/11/billionaire-tax-gavin-newsom-01070600) for his opposition to Prop 40, which he says would devastate California’s finances (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/newsom-unloads-on-california-wealth-tax-proposal-00723732) by pushing wealthy taxpayers out of the state. And if Prop 42 ends up blocking the tax over the will of the voters, it would only give more fuel to critics accusing the governor of carrying the billionaires’ water.
Rep. Ro Khanna has hammered that point as he and Newsom circle each other ahead of a potential presidential matchup. Khanna has leaned into the wealth tax as a way to both bolster his progressive bona fides and differentiate himself from Newsom, and he has excoriated Newsom for backing Prop 42.
“If a majority of Californians vote yes on Prop 40, that’s a mandate to make billionaires pay their fair share,” Khanna said in a statement to Playbook. “Overturning that through the billionaire-funded loophole that Governor Newsom is championing would be a betrayal of the voters who fought for this. The Democratic Party has to decide whether it stands with working people or with the donor class. I know which side I’m on.”
Advertisements for Prop 42 do not directly link the proposal to the billionaires tax. Proponents are instead emphasizing the other main component of the measure: a prohibition on new taxes on financial assets such as stocks and retirement accounts.
“Californians should never have to worry that politicians will come after the retirement savings they spent a lifetime earning. Yet five proposals in recent years show that the threat is real,” said Brian Marvel , president of the law enforcement union Peace Officer Resource Association of California, which has endorsed the initiative. “Prop 40 is just the latest example of this emerging threat. …Whatever happens with Prop 40, Prop 42 gives Californians the long-term protection they deserve.”
But to Prop 40 backers, Prop 42 is inextricable from the efforts to quash the billionaire tax. The fact that deep-pocketed opponents funding the anti-Prop 40 campaign have spent nearly $40 million on advertising for a second measure that could kill the tax illustrates the lengths they are willing to go — and the resources they have at hand. (The same group behind Prop 42 also qualified a second measure, Proposition 41, which has been largely abandoned.)
Newsom did not elaborate on his reasons for backing Prop 42 when he rolled out his endorsements this month, but people close to him say his position is an extension of his long-standing opposition to a state-level wealth tax.
Some members of Newsom’s orbit acknowledge the potential of both measures passing could be politically explosive, but said it’s not a particularly pressing concern, mainly because they are increasingly certain the billionaires tax will fail. Private polling from three separate polling firms — FM3, Public Opinion Strategies and Binder Research — have consistently shown the measure hovering in the high 30s or low 40s, well short of the majority it would need to pass.
That is a notable divergence from public polls, which have regularly shown Prop 40 with a slight edge, usually with a plurality that falls short of 50%. That is a precarious place for a ballot measure (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) in the closing weeks of an election, but a more optimistic view than the opponents’ internals.
If the measure does pass, the political blast radius could be vast. It would be a jolt to the Democratic political establishment — including gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and powerful interest groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood — which led its imprimatur to the ‘no’ side. It would put billionaires like Brin and other ‘no on 40’ funders on notice that populist fury at growing wealth inequality is strong enough to overcome a deluge of political spending.
And for Newsom, it would put him on a losing side of the issue, even as he has called for raising taxes on billionaires on a national level (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/26/newsom-calls-for-national-billionaires-tax-00977751) and has struck other populist notes, including backing public equity stakes in the profits generated by artificial intelligence companies.
SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez blasted Newsom for abetting what she called a cynical scheme to disenfranchise millions of voters, calling Prop 42 a “misleading and dangerous threat to Californians.”
“Governor Newsom is in lockstep with his billionaire-backers,” Jimenez said in a statement. “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors: he’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask 200 billionaires to finally pay their fair share.”

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (left), and Randy Villegas, Democratic candidate for congress in California's 22nd District, wave at the end of a campaign rally on Oct. 23, 2026, in Bakersfield, California. | Jae C. Hong/AP
CLASS FOCUS — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made no mention of Prop 40 or the measures meant to undercut it as she rallied for progressive House candidate Randy Villegas in Bakersfield on Friday.
She didn’t spend much time discussing her and Villegas’ similar ideological profiles, either. Instead, the potential presidential candidate, who has not endorsed the wealth tax, emphasized their working class origins, saying Villegas’ family’s story, immigrating from Mexico and starting an auto body shop, was the “American dream at work, where we start from nothing and we make something of ourselves.”
She compared his upbringing, working in the shop before becoming a political science professor, to hers, helping her mom clean houses growing up.

Villegas echoed the class-based appeals that have become foundational to their wing of the Democratic Party, while railing against Speaker Mike Johnson ’s recent visit to the Central Valley to campaign alongside his opponent, Rep. David Valadao . He urged attendees to tell their family members to vote, before joking: “Call your ex. Make sure they get their ballot in, but only if they’re going to vote for us, right?”
RELATED: AOC stops by In-N-Out burger during California campaign trip (https://nypost.com/2026/10/24/us-news/aoc-stops-by-in-n-out-burger-during-california-campaign-trip/) by the California Post’s Geoff Earle
Rep. Mike Thompson speaks with reporters after a news conference on Sept. 30, 2025, in Washington. | Mariam Zuhaib/AP
STAFF SPAT — The intra-party fight between Rep. Mike Thompson and challenger Eric Jones has spilled into a dispute between Thompson’s former staffers. The dust-up began when Jones released an ad (https://x.com/andrewsolender/status/2114083961836089529?s=46) featuring Thompson’s former communications director, T.J. Adams-Falconer , accusing the Democratic representative of being in office too long and part of a “corrupt political system.”
“Mike Thompson told me directly he plans to die in office,” Adams-Falconer says, before saying he’ll be voting for Jones. The ad shows a photo of Adams-Falconer standing next to the congressmember, along with other staff members.
The Thompson campaign responded with a letter from seven of those former staffers who take issue with Adams-Falconer’s assertion and are demanding the Jones campaign remove the image from the ad.
“Collectively, we have served Congressman Thompson for over thirty years, and none of us have ever heard the Congressman say anything of the kind,” the letter reads. “What we have heard him say is precisely the opposite — that he does NOT intend to die in office.”
Meanwhile, the Thompson campaign is hitting Jones for pouring more of his personal wealth into the contest. Jones loaned his campaign roughly $5 million this month, according to FEC filings, bringing his total investment in the race to nearly $15 million.
“Voters will not be deceived by a San Francisco venture capitalist air dropping into our communities to buy a seat in Congress,” Thomas Dowling , Thompson’s campaign manager, said in a statement.
ON THE HILL
House Financial Services Committee Ranking Member Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) walks to a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, on June 9, 2026. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WATERED DOWN — The center-left Majority Democrats, which represents younger Democratic officials, deleted a post criticizing Rep. Maxine Waters , 88, and the Capitol Hill “gerontocracy,” Jasper Goodman reports (https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/10/23/congress/democratic-group-walks-back-gerontocracy-swipe-against-maxine-waters-01134350). The deletion came after one of the group’s members, Rep. Ritchie Torres , pushed back against the post that appeared to take aim at Waters’ campaign to continue as the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee.
STARLINK SLOWDOWN — A trio of House Democrats representing Silicon Valley demanded that the White House investigate reports that SpaceX limited its military-grade version of Starlink satellite services to Ukrainians on the battlefield, writes Owen Dahlkamp (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/23/starshield-slowdown-probe-democrats-01133720).
In a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles , Reps. Sam Liccardo , Jimmy Panetta and Khanna asked for a briefing within two weeks outlining who decided to restrict Starshield speeds, how they were implemented and if any contractual obligations were violated. The lawmakers also asked for details of whether similar vulnerabilities exist elsewhere.
The Wall Street Journal has reported (https://www.wsj.com/world/ukraine-starlink-elon-musk-trump-dbc49193) that Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of Starlink and that he spoke with President Donald Trump and other senior administration officials before the limits were imposed.
DOWN THE BALLOT
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: DOWNSTREAM IMPACT — A candidate in the typically sleepy race for Board of Equalization is trying to ride the wave of spending in battleground congressional districts as he seeks to flip the state’s only Republican-held constitutional office and seat on the panel. The campaign for Fresno City Councilmember Nelson Esparza , in a memo set for distribution to prospective donors, party leaders and labor unions, argued that the 1st BOE district’s overlap with the competitive districts of Valadao and Rep. Adam Gray , and its slight Democratic voter registration edge, make it prime for a flip. Esparza is facing term-limited state Sen. Shannon Grove for the open seat, which is currently held by Republican Ted Gaines .
OLYMPIC GAMES
CARRYING THE FLAME — San Jose is pushing to be a torch city during the 2028 Olympics, vying for a chance to have the Olympic flame cross through the city on its way to Los Angeles. The torch will move through all 50 states for the first time during the LA games, according to Mayor Matt Mahan ’s office, with its final path announced next year. The city’s council is set to consider the proposal on Nov. 3.
CALIFORNIA CURRENTS
PACK YOUR BAGS — Climate-related disasters have forced thousands of Californians out of their homes in the last few years. Some have moved to new communities, while others have left the state, and experts are warning that this is merely the beginning. Newsom’s poison-pill problem
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones)
10/26/2026 09:00 AM EDT
California Gov. Gavin Newsom attends a rally with members of the state's Democratic Party, organized labor, and other advocates in San Francisco, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. | Heather Diehl/AP
DOUBLE TROUBLE — If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to Gavin Newsom . But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible. One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%. And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
Newsom, a likely presidential contender, already has taken considerable political heat (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/11/billionaire-tax-gavin-newsom-01070600) for his opposition to Prop 40, which he says would devastate California’s finances (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/newsom-unloads-on-california-wealth-tax-proposal-00723732) by pushing wealthy taxpayers out of the state. And if Prop 42 ends up blocking the tax over the will of the voters, it would only give more fuel to critics accusing the governor of carrying the billionaires’ water.
Rep. Ro Khanna has hammered that point as he and Newsom circle each other ahead of a potential presidential matchup. Khanna has leaned into the wealth tax as a way to both bolster his progressive bona fides and differentiate himself from Newsom, and he has excoriated Newsom for backing Prop 42.
“If a majority of Californians vote yes on Prop 40, that’s a mandate to make billionaires pay their fair share,” Khanna said in a statement to Playbook. “Overturning that through the billionaire-funded loophole that Governor Newsom is championing would be a betrayal of the voters who fought for this. The Democratic Party has to decide whether it stands with working people or with the donor class. I know which side I’m on.”
Advertisements for Prop 42 do not directly link the proposal to the billionaires tax. Proponents are instead emphasizing the other main component of the measure: a prohibition on new taxes on financial assets such as stocks and retirement accounts.
“Californians should never have to worry that politicians will come after the retirement savings they spent a lifetime earning. Yet five proposals in recent years show that the threat is real,” said Brian Marvel , president of the law enforcement union Peace Officer Resource Association of California, which has endorsed the initiative. “Prop 40 is just the latest example of this emerging threat. …Whatever happens with Prop 40, Prop 42 gives Californians the long-term protection they deserve.”
But to Prop 40 backers, Prop 42 is inextricable from the efforts to quash the billionaire tax. The fact that deep-pocketed opponents funding the anti-Prop 40 campaign have spent nearly $40 million on advertising for a second measure that could kill the tax illustrates the lengths they are willing to go — and the resources they have at hand. (The same group behind Prop 42 also qualified a second measure, Proposition 41, which has been largely abandoned.)
Newsom did not elaborate on his reasons for backing Prop 42 when he rolled out his endorsements this month, but people close to him say his position is an extension of his long-standing opposition to a state-level wealth tax.
Some members of Newsom’s orbit acknowledge the potential of both measures passing could be politically explosive, but said it’s not a particularly pressing concern, mainly because they are increasingly certain the billionaires tax will fail. Private polling from three separate polling firms — FM3, Public Opinion Strategies and Binder Research — have consistently shown the measure hovering in the high 30s or low 40s, well short of the majority it would need to pass.
That is a notable divergence from public polls, which have regularly shown Prop 40 with a slight edge, usually with a plurality that falls short of 50%. That is a precarious place for a ballot measure (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) in the closing weeks of an election, but a more optimistic view than the opponents’ internals.
If the measure does pass, the political blast radius could be vast. It would be a jolt to the Democratic political establishment — including gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and powerful interest groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood — which led its imprimatur to the ‘no’ side. It would put billionaires like Brin and other ‘no on 40’ funders on notice that populist fury at growing wealth inequality is strong enough to overcome a deluge of political spending.
And for Newsom, it would put him on a losing side of the issue, even as he has called for raising taxes on billionaires on a national level (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/26/newsom-calls-for-national-billionaires-tax-00977751) and has struck other populist notes, including backing public equity stakes in the profits generated by artificial intelligence companies.
SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez blasted Newsom for abetting what she called a cynical scheme to disenfranchise millions of voters, calling Prop 42 a “misleading and dangerous threat to Californians.”
“Governor Newsom is in lockstep with his billionaire-backers,” Jimenez said in a statement. “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors: he’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask 200 billionaires to finally pay their fair share.”
