CAMPAIGN YEAR
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (left), and Randy Villegas, Democratic candidate for congress in California's 22nd District, wave at the end of a campaign rally on Oct. 23, 2026, in Bakersfield, California. | Jae C. Hong/AP
CLASS FOCUS — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made no mention of Prop 40 or the measures meant to undercut it as she rallied for progressive House candidate Randy Villegas in Bakersfield on Friday.
She didn’t spend much time discussing her and Villegas’ similar ideological profiles, either. Instead, the potential presidential candidate, who has not endorsed the wealth tax, emphasized their working class origins, saying Villegas’ family’s story, immigrating from Mexico and starting an auto body shop, was the “American dream at work, where we start from nothing and we make something of ourselves.”
She compared his upbringing, working in the shop before becoming a political science professor, to hers, helping her mom clean houses growing up.

Villegas echoed the class-based appeals that have become foundational to their wing of the Democratic Party, while railing against Speaker Mike Johnson ’s recent visit to the Central Valley to campaign alongside his opponent, Rep. David Valadao . He urged attendees to tell their family members to vote, before joking: “Call your ex. Make sure they get their ballot in, but only if they’re going to vote for us, right?”
RELATED: AOC stops by In-N-Out burger during California campaign trip (https://nypost.com/2026/10/24/us-news/aoc-stops-by-in-n-out-burger-during-california-campaign-trip/) by the California Post’s Geoff Earle
Rep. Mike Thompson speaks with reporters after a news conference on Sept. 30, 2025, in Washington. | Mariam Zuhaib/AP
STAFF SPAT — The intra-party fight between Rep. Mike Thompson and challenger Eric Jones has spilled into a dispute between Thompson’s former staffers. The dust-up began when Jones released an ad (https://x.com/andrewsolender/status/2114083961836089529?s=46) featuring Thompson’s former communications director, T.J. Adams-Falconer , accusing the Democratic representative of being in office too long and part of a “corrupt political system.”
“Mike Thompson told me directly he plans to die in office,” Adams-Falconer says, before saying he’ll be voting for Jones. The ad shows a photo of Adams-Falconer standing next to the congressmember, along with other staff members.
The Thompson campaign responded with a letter from seven of those former staffers who take issue with Adams-Falconer’s assertion and are demanding the Jones campaign remove the image from the ad.
“Collectively, we have served Congressman Thompson for over thirty years, and none of us have ever heard the Congressman say anything of the kind,” the letter reads. “What we have heard him say is precisely the opposite — that he does NOT intend to die in office.”
Meanwhile, the Thompson campaign is hitting Jones for pouring more of his personal wealth into the contest. Jones loaned his campaign roughly $5 million this month, according to FEC filings, bringing his total investment in the race to nearly $15 million.
“Voters will not be deceived by a San Francisco venture capitalist air dropping into our communities to buy a seat in Congress,” Thomas Dowling , Thompson’s campaign manager, said in a statement.
ON THE HILL
House Financial Services Committee Ranking Member Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) walks to a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, on June 9, 2026. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WATERED DOWN — The center-left Majority Democrats, which represents younger Democratic officials, deleted a post criticizing Rep. Maxine Waters , 88, and the Capitol Hill “gerontocracy,” Jasper Goodman reports (https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/10/23/congress/democratic-group-walks-back-gerontocracy-swipe-against-maxine-waters-01134350). The deletion came after one of the group’s members, Rep. Ritchie Torres , pushed back against the post that appeared to take aim at Waters’ campaign to continue as the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee.
STARLINK SLOWDOWN — A trio of House Democrats representing Silicon Valley demanded that the White House investigate reports that SpaceX limited its military-grade version of Starlink satellite services to Ukrainians on the battlefield, writes Owen Dahlkamp (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/23/starshield-slowdown-probe-democrats-01133720).
In a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles , Reps. Sam Liccardo , Jimmy Panetta and Khanna asked for a briefing within two weeks outlining who decided to restrict Starshield speeds, how they were implemented and if any contractual obligations were violated. The lawmakers also asked for details of whether similar vulnerabilities exist elsewhere.
The Wall Street Journal has reported (https://www.wsj.com/world/ukraine-starlink-elon-musk-trump-dbc49193) that Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of Starlink and that he spoke with President Donald Trump and other senior administration officials before the limits were imposed.
DOWN THE BALLOT
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: DOWNSTREAM IMPACT — A candidate in the typically sleepy race for Board of Equalization is trying to ride the wave of spending in battleground congressional districts as he seeks to flip the state’s only Republican-held constitutional office and seat on the panel. The campaign for Fresno City Councilmember Nelson Esparza , in a memo set for distribution to prospective donors, party leaders and labor unions, argued that the 1st BOE district’s overlap with the competitive districts of Valadao and Rep. Adam Gray , and its slight Democratic voter registration edge, make it prime for a flip. Esparza is facing term-limited state Sen. Shannon Grove for the open seat, which is currently held by Republican Ted Gaines .

CARRYING THE FLAME — San Jose is pushing to be a torch city during the 2028 Olympics, vying for a chance to have the Olympic flame cross through the city on its way to Los Angeles. The torch will move through all 50 states for the first time during the LA games, according to Mayor Matt Mahan ’s office, with its final path announced next year. The city’s council is set to consider the proposal on Nov. 3.

I'm looking at the prediction-market prices as of the evening of Nov 2: Kalshi has Prop 42 near 56%, Polymarket at 54%, so it reads as a toss-up. The earlier Oct 29 figures, around 79–80%, don't line up with that, which makes me suspect different dates or a big market swing.

The Nov 2 toss-up price looks like a sharp move from the roughly 80% readings on Oct 29, which I'd guess came from the Berkeley poll released that day. Both markets now lean slightly toward Yes, around 55–57%, while the recent polls suggest a tie or a slight No, so I'm weighing which signal to trust.

I'm weighing whether the markets or the polls are the better guide here. Markets on ballot measures are thin and can lean toward the "no new taxes" framing that appeals to their trader base, so I'm doubting that the roughly 55% Yes reading tells the whole story.

I'm weighing the polls against the market prices: the PPIC poll has Yes ahead 51–47, while Berkeley has No ahead 43–45, which averages to roughly a tie among decided voters. I'm also considering whether undecided voters on ballot measures usually break toward No, since that status-quo pattern could move the result away from the market's 55% Yes reading.

I'm weighing whether the Democratic share of the electorate and the early-vote share change how the PPIC and Berkeley numbers should be read, since a turnout model could tilt the Yes lead one way or the other.

I'm weighing the Yes side's pitch about protecting retirement savings and avoiding new taxes against the "poison pill" framing that could make voters balk. Democrats may be getting party cues to vote No, and Republicans and independents leaned Yes in September, so the partisan split matters a lot here.

I'm weighing the cost of the No campaign's late spending against the Yes side's fundraising edge, and checking how Prop 41 has been polling as a comparable measure.

I'm weighing the On Point model's 50.7% Yes estimate against the polls, which suggests Prop 42 is closer to a coin flip than the 56.9% chance the model gives it. Undecided voters on measures like this often break toward No, so the adjusted Yes share could land near 49–50%, and the gap comes down to how On Point averages the September polling.

I'm checking whether the On Point model's Yes lean holds up, since the fundamentals might favor No in a Democratic-leaning midterm, and I'm weighing how the county-level projections fit that picture. I'm also starting to compare how prediction markets and polls diverge on measures like this.

I'm comparing the Oct 29 prices of roughly 79–80% with the Nov 2 figures near 55%, and wondering whether the NY Post numbers were stale or accurate. A drop of about 25 points in four days would fit the Berkeley poll landing on Oct 29 and pulling the market toward No.

I'm checking the defirate snapshots next, since they list Prop 42 at different prices (57% on Kalshi against 92¢ on Polymarket in one listing) and that inconsistency makes me trust the Nov 2 reading of about 55% more than the rest.

The market and the model both put Prop 42's Yes side slightly ahead, around 55–57%, but the polls lean closer to a tie, so I want to check whether anyone has analyzed the outcome directly before deciding which signal to trust. I'm going to look for expert commentary on whether Prop 42 is likely to pass.

I'm going to look for analysis of whether Prop 42 is expected to pass, and I'll check the Politico piece on Newsom's poison-pill problem, since it may cite private polling on the measure.

I'm tallying the campaign spending: the Yes side has about $159.1M, while the No side has roughly $34.5M, mostly from SEIU, so the gap is around 4.6 to 1 and still growing.

Now I'm weighing the non-financial factors: the Yes side leans on a popular retirement-savings message, while the No side is mostly labor-driven and focused on Prop 40.

I'm now checking the latest polls, which show Yes slipping slightly while No has climbed, and the prediction markets and forecast models that put Yes a bit ahead.

I'm weighing the historical angle now: whether a big spending edge usually carries a ballot measure, and whether low-information measures are more swayed by money. Leaning toward Yes at about 55%, since the markets and the On Point model point that way while the polls are mixed, though I'm wary that thin ballot-measure markets may be skewed.

I'm weighing whether the market's drop from about 80% to 55% reflects new information, like the IGS poll, or just thin trading. Either way, I'm reading 55% as a slight Yes lean, and I'm wondering whether the market's view on the final stretch could be more informed.

I'm checking for any late-breaking news from November 1 and 2 that might have shifted the picture, such as endorsement fallout, last-minute ads, or closing arguments on Prop 42.

# Proposition 42
## Should California prohibit new taxes on financial assets like stocks and investment accounts and prohibit most retroactive taxes?
This would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property.
It also prohibits most retroactive taxes.
Both of those provisions conflict with the wealth tax on billionaires proposed by Proposition 40, which seeks to tax financial assets and is retroactive to Jan. 1 of this year.
If both measures pass and Proposition 42 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, it’s likely the billionaire tax would not be enacted.
## Yes Argument
Californians already pay income tax and shouldn’t also be taxed on money sitting in investment accounts.
This measure closes a loophole to protect average people’s life savings and prohibits a change in rules after the fact by barring unfair retroactive taxes.
## No Argument
This is another attempt to invalidate the billionaire wealth tax, disguised as a measure to protect the retirement accounts of average Californians.
While average people pay income tax on their wages, billionaires’ wealth grows mainly through the rising value of stock they already hold, and they don’t have to pay taxes on those assets until they cash them out.
Proposition 40 wouldn’t impose taxes on retirement accounts of anyone other than those of billionaires.

# Proposition 42
## Should California prohibit new taxes on financial assets like stocks and investment accounts and prohibit most retroactive taxes?
This would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property.
It also prohibits most retroactive taxes.
Both of those provisions conflict with the wealth tax on billionaires proposed by Proposition 40, which seeks to tax financial assets and is retroactive to Jan. 1 of this year.
If both measures pass and Proposition 42 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, it’s likely the billionaire tax would not be enacted.
## Yes Argument
Californians already pay income tax and shouldn’t also be taxed on money sitting in investment accounts.
This measure closes a loophole to protect average people’s life savings and prohibits a change in rules after the fact by barring unfair retroactive taxes.
## No Argument
This is another attempt to invalidate the billionaire wealth tax, disguised as a measure to protect the retirement accounts of average Californians.
While average people pay income tax on their wages, billionaires’ wealth grows mainly through the rising value of stock they already hold, and they don’t have to pay taxes on those assets until they cash them out.
Proposition 40 wouldn’t impose taxes on retirement accounts of anyone other than those of billionaires.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The so-called billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) has become one of the most contested California propositions in years, generating national interest and massive spending by opponents (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax). It also has spawned two rival ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Here’s a cheat sheet for sorting it all out.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some ofCalifornia’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they are spending a fortune to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.

Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)

Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.

I'm weighing the historical angle now: whether a big spending edge usually carries a ballot measure, and whether low-information measures are more swayed by money. # Proposition 42
## Should California prohibit new taxes on financial assets like stocks and investment accounts and prohibit most retroactive taxes?
This would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property.
It also prohibits most retroactive taxes.
Both of those provisions conflict with the wealth tax on billionaires proposed by Proposition 40, which seeks to tax financial assets and is retroactive to Jan. 1 of this year.
If both measures pass and Proposition 42 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, it’s likely the billionaire tax would not be enacted.
## Yes Argument
Californians already pay income tax and shouldn’t also be taxed on money sitting in investment accounts.
This measure closes a loophole to protect average people’s life savings and prohibits a change in rules after the fact by barring unfair retroactive taxes.
## No Argument
This is another attempt to invalidate the billionaire wealth tax, disguised as a measure to protect the retirement accounts of average Californians.
While average people pay income tax on their wages, billionaires’ wealth grows mainly through the rising value of stock they already hold, and they don’t have to pay taxes on those assets until they cash them out.
Proposition 40 wouldn’t impose taxes on retirement accounts of anyone other than those of billionaires.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The so-called billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) has become one of the most contested California propositions in years, generating national interest and massive spending by opponents (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax). It also has spawned two rival ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Here’s a cheat sheet for sorting it all out.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some ofCalifornia’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they are spending a fortune to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.

I'm checking the LA Times piece, though the middle section on Prop 42's pros and cons sits past what I've read so far. The article's framing of a likely Democratic-leaning environment suggests a larger Democratic turnout, which would weigh against the Yes side's chances.

I'm checking the electorate math on Prop 42: a Dem-heavy sample would push the Yes share toward 49%, while a more balanced one gives about 51%. Since the outcome swings on the partisan mix, this looks close to a coin flip.

The markets and models both lean toward Yes, while the polls sit close to 50/50 with the most recent readings drifting down for Yes. I'm still unsure what the question wants, since "answer with only yes or no" could mean either side is the one more likely to win.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side actually wins: the markets and the forecast model both sit around 55-57% for Yes, and the spending edge helps, but the polls drifting toward No and the Democratic-leaning environment could cut the other way. I'm also recalling how well prediction markets have tracked California ballot measures in past cycles, since that affects how much weight I give the market price.

I'm comparing the historical accuracy of prediction markets on California ballot measures, where some markets were well calibrated and others missed. Taking the market price at around 55% and the model at 57%, I'm leaning toward a slight edge for Yes, even though the polls and Democratic opposition argue the other way.

I'm weighing the Yes side's chances against the pollsters' point that undecided voters tend to break toward No. The markets and the On Point model still put Yes around 55-57%, which suggests a narrow edge for Yes. I'm also considering whether other polls or late independent spending might shift that estimate.

I'm now estimating turnout for the November midterm, roughly 55-60% of registered voters. I'm also checking how PPIC's likely-voter sample and turnout models have fared on past California propositions, including the 2022 Prop 30, 27, and 1 results.

I'm checking how PPIC's final results compared with their October polls on past propositions: in 2022 Prop 27 finished well below what the polls showed, while Prop 28 came in a few points higher. For 2020 I'm noting that PPIC's last poll often overstated the Yes side on some measures, such as Prop 16, where the final result came in lower.

I'm checking how PPIC's final results from 2020 compared with their polls: some measures like Prop 16 and Prop 15 finished below what the last poll showed, while others like Prop 22 and Prop 24 finished higher. The pattern looks mixed, so I don't see a consistent bias in their Yes numbers.

I'm going back over PPIC's past October numbers against their final results, and Prop 35 and 36 finished well above what they showed, while Props 32, 33, 34 and 5 landed close to or just under. So their final readings have been fairly reliable. Given Prop 42 sitting around 51% with a downward drift, I'd expect the final result to land somewhere near 48 to 50%.

The IGS reading of 43% Yes with 12% undecided points to a final result near 47–49%, and averaging that with PPIC gives roughly 48–50% Yes. That makes it close to a coin flip with a slight lean toward failing, which sits awkwardly against the markets at 55%. Heavy Yes-side spending might still pull the result above the polls, as it did with Prop 22 in 2020, while the No side leans on party and labor messaging.

I'm weighing whether to go with the Yes side based on the evidence, though it still looks close to a coin flip. The question is only a binary call, and since the result isn't known yet, I need to pick whichever side the evidence favors.

I'm comparing the prediction market prices with the forecast model and the spending gap, where the Yes side has far more money behind it. The PPIC poll at 51-47 for Yes and the mixed endorsements, including Newsom's, keep me from reading this as a clear call.

I'm now weighing the evidence for the No side: Berkeley IGS shows Yes slipping from a tie to a No lead with 12% undecided, PPIC has Yes sliding while No climbs, and the Democratic Party, labor, and a poison-pill framing all push against it.

I'm weighing the markets, which lean Yes, against the polls, which have been drifting toward No and undecided voters often break that way. The Yes side's spending edge and the trend in the forecast model make this a close call, and I'm treating the market price as a reasonable signal even though the On Point model is an unfamiliar source.

I'm weighing whether it's worth checking the early-vote composition on the On Point site, since it could show how Democrat-heavy the electorate is. Still, it feels like a tangent next to the polls and markets I've already gone through.

I'm thinking about whether the early-vote composition could reveal how Democrat-heavy the electorate is, and whether older, Yes-leaning early voters might push the result up. The Berkeley IGS October numbers don't show older voters' Yes share, though, so I can't tell how much that would help.

I'm looking for the Berkeley IGS late-October crosstabs on Prop 42 by age or party, since the PDF itself is blocked. I'll check whether any news coverage reports the party breakdown, and also look at CalMatters' voter guide for what the polls show.

I'm going to search for whether Prop 42 is being reported as favored to pass, checking for articles that cite the markets or call it likely to pass.

# Newsom’s poison-pill problem
**DOUBLE TROUBLE —** If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to **Gavin Newsom**.
But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.

If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible.
One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%.
And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
...

...

# Newsom’s poison-pill problem
**DOUBLE TROUBLE —** If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to **Gavin Newsom**.
But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder **Sergey Brin** and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets.
If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible.
One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%.
And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
